newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish PM says coalition seeks early elections.
newsitem.headline: Turkish PM says coalition seeks early elections.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan said on Sunday his crumbling 11-month-old coalition had decided to seek early elections to solve a government crisis.

The deputy prime minister Tansu Ciller, leader of the junior coalition member - the True Path Party (DYP) - said she would lead a caretakeover government from the end of June until the elections take place.
Erbakan told a news conference, "We decided that for Turkey to continue its economic success, an early election would be necessary."

Erbakan's party has been locked in bargaining with the DYP over a possible date for early elections, which must be approved by parliament. A DYP minister has said elections could be held as early as October.

However, the two sides have been unable to agree on a date. Turkish press reports say Erbakan wants a quick poll, but Ciller was holding out for a date next spring. Elections would normally be due by the year 2000.
Ciller, appearing with Erbakan, said polls would take place within a "reasonable" time to end the crisis, touched off by army demands for a crackdown on Islamist activism.
"It was seen as suitable to go to elections in a reasonable time...The prime ministership will change hands by the end of the month," Ciller said.
Under the government protocol Ciller was originally due to take over the prime minister's office in June 1998.

The coalition's position in parliament has been undermined by a series of defections culminating in the resignation of a senior True Path deputy on Friday which left the government one seat short of the 276 votes needed for an absolute majority.
Erbakan said he expected the coalition parties to emerge stronger from national polls.
"We believe we (the coalition partners) will come back stronger if we go to elections," the Islamist leader said.
The army, spearheading an attack by Turkey's traditional secularist elite, first challenged Erbakan at the National Security Council's February meeting to move against his own grassroots supporters.
So far Erbakan has dragged his feet, setting him at odds with Ciller's conservative and secularist party members.
The result has been a steady flow of defections of True Path MPs and ministers -- all decrying Erbakan's failure to implement the army directives.
